name: Silky Zubat 13" Curved Hand Saw
title: Silky Zubat 13" Curved Hand Saw for Arborists
meta: The Silky Zubat 13-inch curved hand saw: aggressive pull-stroke teeth, replaceable blade and a scabbard that rides on a saddle. Specs, sizing and use tips.
tagline: A 330 mm curved pull saw for climbers who prune and remove limbs all day.
summary: The Silky Zubat is the curved hand saw a lot of climbers reach for once a branch is too big for pruners but too small to justify the top-handle. The 330 mm blade cuts fast on the pull stroke and the curve keeps the teeth biting when you are reaching overhead. It rides in its own scabbard on the saddle and takes a replacement blade when the teeth are done.
highlights: 330 mm (13 in) curved blade that cuts on the pull stroke
Large impulse-hardened teeth for fast cuts in green wood
Curve holds the saw in the kerf on overhead and reaching cuts
Rubberized handle with a lanyard hole
Replaceable blade, so the handle and scabbard keep going
Scabbard included, belt or saddle mount

body.h: Where the Zubat earns its spot on the saddle
p: On a prune or a crown clean, most cuts are in the 1 to 4 inch range. That is exactly where a Silky saw zubat pays off. The curved blade pulls itself into the wood, so you are not muscling it from an awkward position, and the long stroke means fewer passes before the limb drops.

Because it cuts on the pull, the blade stays in tension and is less likely to buckle when you are working at arm's length. Climbers who do a lot of reduction work like that it lets them make clean cuts at the branch collar without starting the saw. It is also the saw you want for dead-wooding near a client's roof, where a chainsaw is more noise and risk than the job needs.

The Zubat uses big, aggressive teeth that remove wood quickly in green hardwood and softwood. The cut finish is rougher than a fine-tooth pruning saw, but on most arborist work speed matters more than a glassy face. If you do a lot of fine ornamental pruning, keep a smaller saw for that work and use the Zubat for anything structural.

The teeth are impulse-hardened, which keeps them sharp a long time but means they are not meant to be filed. When the blade gets dull or kinked, swap in a replacement blade. The handle and scabbard last through several blades if you look after them.

Compared with straight-blade saws, the curve has another advantage: it keeps the cutting edge in contact with the wood as your arm swings through its natural arc. You get more cutting per stroke and less skating on the bark, which is why the Zubat is a common pick for anyone asking for a dedicated silky arborist saw.

The scabbard has a belt loop and clips onto most saddles. Mount it on the side opposite your lanyard so the handle is easy to reach without tangling. A short tether through the handle hole is cheap insurance if you work over a driveway, a pool or people on the ground. Keep the saw sheathed whenever you are moving through the tree, and keep your climbing line and lanyard out of the cutting path, since a sharp pull saw goes through rope as easily as wood.
For more options, see our full range of hand saws and scabbards, including straight blades and longer saws for removal work.

body.h: Who should buy the Silky Zubat pruning saw
p: If you climb for a living and your current hand saw is slowing you down, this is the standard upgrade. Ground workers clearing brush and plant health care crews doing structural pruning also get a lot out of it. Beginners do fine with it too, but respect the teeth: they will open up a glove or a leg in a hurry, so keep cuts away from your body and your lines.

faq.q: Can I sharpen the Silky Zubat blade?
faq.a: Not practically. The teeth are impulse-hardened and are designed to be replaced rather than filed. Replacement blades fit the original handle.

faq.q: Is the Zubat good for climbing work?
faq.a: Yes. It is one of the most common arborist saws on a saddle because it cuts fast, rides in a secure scabbard and is light enough to carry all day.

faq.q: What size branches does it handle best?
faq.a: It is most efficient on limbs from about 1 to 6 inches. Beyond that, a top-handle chainsaw is usually the faster and safer choice.

faq.q: Does it cut on the push stroke?
faq.a: No. Like most Japanese-style saws, the Zubat cuts on the pull. Let the pull do the work and use the push stroke only to reset.

name: Notch Nobasu 20' 4-Section Telescoping Aluminum Polesaw
title: Notch Nobasu 20' 4-Section Telescoping Aluminum Polesaw
meta: Notch Nobasu 20' 4-section telescoping aluminum polesaw: reach high limbs from the ground, collapse it for the truck. How it works, specs and safe use.
tagline: A four-section telescoping pole saw that reaches about 20 feet from the ground.
summary: The Notch Nobasu 20' 4-section telescoping aluminum polesaw is built for ground-based pruning when the limb is out of reach of a hand saw and a climb is not worth it. Four aluminum sections slide out to about 20 feet and collapse back down for the truck. A pull-stroke blade does the cutting, so you guide the saw rather than fight it.
highlights: Extends to about 20 feet in four telescoping sections
Aluminum pole keeps weight down for overhead work
Collapses short for storage on the truck or in the shop
Pull-stroke blade for clean, controlled cuts
Good for clearance pruning, deadwood and raising canopies

body.h: What a telescoping polesaw is for
p: A lot of pruning never needs a climber. Lifting a canopy over a sidewalk, taking deadwood out of a street tree, clearing a limb off a roof: a good pole saw handles those from the ground in a few minutes. The Nobasu stretches to about 20 feet, and with your own reach that covers most of the low and mid canopy on residential work.
Telescoping matters because you rarely need full length. You run it out only as far as the cut needs, which keeps the saw lighter at the head and easier to control. Shorter is always more accurate.

Telescoping also helps when you move between cuts. Instead of stopping to add or remove a section, you unlock, slide and relock. On a day of lifting street trees, that adds up to a lot of saved time and fewer trips back to the truck.

At full extension, any pole saw gets whippy. Stand off to the side of the limb, not under it, and plan where the piece will fall before you start. Make a small undercut first on anything heavier than a wrist so the bark does not tear down the stem. Then finish from the top. Let the pull stroke do the work and keep the pushes light.
Lock each section fully before you put load on it, and check the locks again after you change length. Wipe sap and grit off the sections at the end of the day so they keep sliding smoothly.

An aluminum pole conducts electricity. Do not use this saw anywhere near energized lines. Line-clearance work belongs to qualified line-clearance arborists using dielectric poles and the procedures in ANSI Z133.

Keep the blade sheathed when the saw is on the truck or leaning against a tree. When the teeth stop pulling a clean chip, replace the blade rather than trying to file it. A dull blade makes you push harder, and at 20 feet of leverage that is how cuts wander and poles bend.
Store the pole collapsed and dry. Compare other options in our pole saws and scabbards section, including fiberglass kits for crews that work around utilities.

body.h: Is the Nobasu right for you
p: If you prune from the ground several times a week, or you run a plant health care crew that does light structural work, a long telescoping saw saves a lot of climbs. Homeowners with big yards like it too. If you need sectional poles that can be insulated and inspected for line work, look at a fiberglass system instead.

Pair it with a good hand saw for the cuts you can reach, and a pole pruner for the small sprouts the saw tends to tear. Between the three, most ground-based pruning on a residential job is covered without anyone leaving the ground.

faq.q: How high can I reach with the Nobasu?
faq.a: The pole extends to about 20 feet. Add your own height and arm reach, and you can work limbs in the mid-20-foot range, though accuracy drops as you go higher.

faq.q: Can I use this polesaw near power lines?
faq.a: No. The pole is aluminum and conducts electricity. Keep well clear of all lines and leave that work to qualified line-clearance crews with dielectric tools.

faq.q: Can the blade be replaced?
faq.a: Yes. Treat the blade as a wear item and replace it when it stops cutting cleanly rather than trying to sharpen it.

name: Jameson LS Kit: Pruner, Pole Saw and Poles
title: Jameson Pole Saw and Pruner LS Kit with Poles
h1: Jameson Pole Saw and Pruner LS Kit with Poles
meta: Jameson pole saw and pruner kit with fiberglass poles. One package for ground-based pruning and clearance work. What is in the kit, specs and how crews use it.
tagline: A complete Jameson pole pruner and pole saw kit with fiberglass sectional poles.
summary: This Jameson pole saw kit puts a pruner head, a saw head and fiberglass sectional poles in one package so a crew can start pruning from the ground on day one. The LS series heads lock onto Jameson poles, and you add or remove sections to match the height of the cut.
highlights: Pole pruner head and pole saw in one kit
Fiberglass sectional poles
Add or remove sections to match the job
Ground-based pruning without a climb

p: Most ground-based pruning comes down to two tools: a jameson pole pruner for clean cuts on small stems and a pole saw for anything thicker. This kit gives you both, plus the poles to run them. Snap the pruner on to tip back sprouts or water shoots, then swap to the saw when you hit a limb the pruner cannot close on.
Sectional poles mean you only carry the length you need. Shorter is more accurate and easier on your shoulders, so start short and add a section when the cut demands it.
Jameson pole saws and pruners are a familiar sight on tree crews and utility trucks, so parts and extra poles are easy to find when something wears out.

Fiberglass is the standard for poles because it is strong, stiff and can be made to resist electrical conduction. That does not make any pole safe near energized lines. Only qualified line-clearance arborists should work near utilities, with tools rated, cleaned and tested for that work under ANSI Z133. Keep the poles clean and dry, inspect for cracks, crushed ends and worn fittings, and retire any section that is damaged.
Store the heads with the blade guarded. Browse more pole saws and poles and kits if you want to add length or spare sections.
Keep the pruner rope in good shape and replace it when it frays, and keep the saw blade sharp or replaced. A dull saw on a long pole wanders and makes you push, which is tiring and less precise.

faq.q: Can I add more poles to a Jameson kit?
faq.a: Yes. Jameson sells extra sections, so you can extend the kit as long as the sections use a matching connection.

faq.q: Are fiberglass poles safe near power lines?
faq.a: Only for qualified line-clearance workers using poles that are rated, clean and tested for that use. Everyone else must stay clear of energized lines.

name: Marvin Cast Saw Head
title: Marvin Cast Saw Head for Pole Saws
meta: Marvin cast saw head for building or repairing a pole saw. Mounts a pruning saw blade to your pole for ground-based cuts. Fit, specs and care tips inside.
tagline: A cast saw head that turns a pole into a pole saw, or replaces a broken one.
summary: The Marvin cast saw head is the fitting that holds a pruning blade on the end of a pole. It is a simple part, but when the old one cracks or the blade wobbles, a new saw head puts your pole saw back in service without buying a whole kit.
highlights: Cast head for mounting a pole saw blade
Replaces a cracked or worn head
Keeps the blade solid on the pole
Simple bolt-on blade mounting

body.h: When to replace a saw head
p: A pole saw takes a beating. Heads get dropped on the truck bed, levered against branch unions and used as a hook to pull hangers down. Over time the casting can crack or the blade seat wears so the blade moves under load. A blade that shifts mid-cut binds, wanders and is hard to control at the end of a long pole.
If the head is cracked, bent, or the blade will not sit tight, replace it. It is a small part that makes the whole tool safer and more accurate.

A good saw head also helps the blade track straight. When the blade seat is worn, the blade can flex sideways in the cut, which leaves a rough face and makes it harder to finish cleanly at the branch collar.

Check that the head matches your pole and blade before you order, since pole fittings vary by maker. Mount the blade with the teeth facing back toward you so it cuts on the pull, and tighten the hardware until there is no play. Recheck it after the first few cuts.

Wipe sap off the head and blade after use and keep the blade guarded in storage. Do not use any pole tool near energized lines unless you are a qualified line-clearance arborist with rated equipment. See more pole saw parts and blades.
Keep a few spare bolts and a wrench in the truck so a loose blade can be tightened on the spot instead of ending the job early.

faq.q: Will this saw head fit my pole?
faq.a: It is made for Marvin pole fittings. Check your pole's connection before ordering, since makers use different fittings.

faq.q: Does the saw head come with a blade?
faq.a: Plan on supplying your own pole saw blade unless the listing says one is included.

name: 6' Foam-Filled Pole
title: Foam Poles: 6' Foam-Filled Fiberglass Pole Section
meta: Foam poles for pole pruners and saws: a 6-foot foam-filled fiberglass section that resists moisture inside the tube. Uses, specs and inspection tips here.
tagline: A 6-foot foam-filled fiberglass pole section for pruner and saw setups.
summary: Foam poles are fiberglass tubes with a foam core, and this 6-foot section is a common building block for pole pruner and pole saw setups. The foam fills the inside of the tube so moisture and dirt cannot collect there, and the pole stays stiff and light enough to work overhead.
highlights: 6-foot fiberglass section
Foam core fills the inside of the tube
Light and stiff for overhead work
Use as a base pole or an extension

p: A hollow fiberglass pole can trap water, condensation and grime on the inside, where you cannot see or clean it. A foam core takes up that space. That is why foam-filled poles are the usual choice for crews who want a pole that stays clean inside, and it is one of the requirements line-clearance outfits look at when they spec tools.
A 6-foot section is a handy length. On its own it works for low pruning and close-in saw work, and stacked with other sections it builds out a longer pole without much flex.
Foam poles are also a little more forgiving of knocks than hollow ones, since the core supports the tube wall. They still need care, but they tend to shrug off the bumps of daily use on the truck.

Keep fiberglass clean and dry. Wipe off sap and dirt after use and store poles off the ground and out of direct sun. Before each job, check for cracks, deep scratches that expose fibers, crushed ends and loose fittings. A damaged pole should come out of service.

No pole makes it safe to work near energized lines unless you are a qualified line-clearance arborist and your tools are rated and tested for that work per ANSI Z133. Find more sections and complete setups in poles and kits.

Keep a record of when each pole entered service and when it was last inspected. On a crew with many poles, a simple numbering system makes it easy to pull a damaged section out before it goes back up a tree.

faq.q: What is the difference between foam-filled and hollow poles?
faq.a: Foam-filled poles have a foam core that keeps moisture and debris out of the tube. Hollow poles are lighter but can collect material inside.

faq.q: Can I connect this pole to other sections?
faq.a: Yes, as long as the fittings match. Check the connection type against your existing poles and heads.

name: Jameson 8' Hollow Core Pole
title: Jameson 8 Foot Pole, Hollow Core Fiberglass
meta: Jameson 8 foot pole, hollow core fiberglass, for pole saws and pruners. A light section to extend your reach for ground pruning. Specs, fit and care tips.
tagline: A light 8-foot Jameson fiberglass section for pole saws and pruners.
summary: This Jameson 8 foot pole is a hollow core fiberglass section for building or extending a pole saw and pruner setup. Hollow construction keeps it light, which matters when you are holding a saw overhead for most of the day.
highlights: 8-foot Jameson fiberglass section
Hollow core for low weight
Use as a base pole or extension
Pairs with Jameson heads and poles

p: Jameson poles are made to connect, so an 8-foot section can be the first pole on a saw or the extra length that gets you to a high limb. Eight feet is long enough to make a real difference in reach while staying manageable on its own.

Hollow core is the lighter option. If you want a pole that stays clean inside, a foam-filled section is the alternative, but for general ground pruning the hollow jameson pole keeps weight off your arms.

Many crews keep a mix of lengths on the truck. An 8-foot section paired with a shorter base pole covers a wide range of heights without carrying more pole than the cut needs. Fewer joints also means less flex at the head.
Check every pole before use for cracks, splintered fibers, crushed ends and worn fittings. Wipe off sap and dirt and store the poles dry and off the ground. Retire any section that is damaged.

A hollow pole is not the choice for work near energized lines. Only qualified line-clearance arborists should work near utilities, with tools rated and tested per ANSI Z133. See matching heads and kits in poles and kits.
If a fitting gets loose or worn, do not tape it up and keep going. A sloppy connection lets the head twist mid-cut and puts extra stress on the fiberglass right at the joint.

faq.q: Does this pole fit other Jameson poles and heads?
faq.a: It is designed for the Jameson system. Confirm your existing fittings match before ordering.

faq.q: Hollow core or foam-filled?
faq.a: Hollow is lighter. Foam-filled keeps moisture and debris out of the tube and is preferred where poles must stay clean inside.

name: Peavey Ash Pole, 12' Long
title: 12 Foot Wood Pole: Peavey Ash Pole for Pole Tools
h1: Peavey Ash Pole: 12 Foot Wood Pole
meta: A 12 foot wood pole in straight-grained ash from Peavey for pole saws and pruners. Traditional feel, solid strength. Specs, uses and safety limits explained.
tagline: A traditional 12-foot ash pole for mounting pole saw and pruner heads.
summary: This 12 foot wood pole is made from ash, the traditional wood for tool handles because it is strong, a little springy and comfortable in the hand. It is a solid base for a pole saw or pruner head when you want a one-piece pole with no joints to work loose.
highlights: 12-foot one-piece ash pole
Strong, shock-absorbing hardwood
No joints to loosen or rattle
Traditional choice for pole tools

p: Ash has been the go-to wood for long handles for generations. It is strong for its weight, flexes a little instead of snapping, and has a feel many workers prefer to fiberglass. A one-piece ash pole has no sections to lock or wear, so there is nothing to rattle when you are working a saw hard.
Twelve feet is a useful length for orchard work, low canopy lifting and clearing hangers from the ground. Fit your pruner or saw head and you have a simple, durable tool.

A one-piece 12 ft wooden pole is also easy to maintain. There are no locks, collars or buttons to fail, and a worn handle can be sanded smooth. For orchard crews and homeowners who prune the same trees every year, it is a simple, long-lived option.
Wood conducts electricity, especially when it is damp. Never use a wooden pole anywhere near power lines. For that, qualified line-clearance arborists use dielectric fiberglass poles under ANSI Z133.
Store the pole dry and flat so it does not bow, and give it a light coat of linseed oil now and then. Check for cracks, splits and loose hardware before use. Compare other options in poles and kits.
Wood can also hide damage. Sight down the pole now and then, look for checks and splits near the ends, and retire it if it starts to bow or crack.

faq.q: Is an ash pole better than fiberglass?
faq.a: It is a matter of use. Ash is affordable, durable and pleasant to handle. Fiberglass is lighter for its length, sectional, and is the only choice for work near utilities.

faq.q: Can I cut a 12 ft wooden pole shorter?
faq.a: Yes, ash can be trimmed, but make sure the end still fits your head's fitting securely.

name: Felco 2 Hand Pruner
title: Felco 2 Hand Pruner: Specs, Sizing and Care
meta: The Felco 2 hand pruner is the classic bypass pruning shear for arborists and gardeners. Specs, who it fits, blade care and replacement parts explained here.
tagline: The classic bypass hand pruner, with replaceable parts that last for years.
summary: The Felco 2 is the bypass hand pruner most tree and landscape crews know by sight. Forged aluminum handles, a hardened steel blade and a design where nearly every part can be replaced make the Felco 2 pruner a tool you buy once and maintain. It cuts green wood up to about an inch cleanly.
highlights: Bypass cut for clean, healthy pruning wounds
Cuts green wood up to about 1 in (25 mm)
Forged aluminum handles
Replaceable blade, anvil blade and spring
Built-in wire cutter
Fits most medium to large hands
specs: Blade, counter blade, spring and more

body.h: Why the Felco 2 is still the standard
p: Hand pruners are the tool you use most and think about least, until a cheap one starts crushing stems and pinching your palm. Felco F2 pruning shears fix both problems. The bypass blade slices past the counter blade like scissors, leaving a clean cut that closes over well, which matters on young trees and ornamentals.

The handles are forged aluminum, light enough to carry on a belt all day and strong enough to take years of use. The geometry is simple and has barely changed in decades, which is a good sign. Crews standardize on it because everyone knows how it feels.

On a tree crew, the Felco 2 pruner is the tool for small clean-up cuts: sprouts at the base, suckers along a trunk, small branches on young trees during a structural prune. It rides in a holster on the belt, and once you are used to it you barely notice it is there.
It is also a good first serious tool for a new ground worker, simple enough to learn quickly and good enough to keep for years.

The Felco 2 is a full-size pruner for medium to large hands. If you have smaller hands or prune all day, the grip span can get tiring, and a smaller model or a rotating-handle version may suit you better. Left-handers should look at a dedicated left-hand model. For most people, though, the Felco pruners 2 are the right place to start.

Use the pruner within its range. Twisting it through a stem that is too thick springs the blades apart and dulls the edge. Switch to loppers or a hand saw like the Silky Zubat once the wood gets past about an inch.

The rubber shock absorber and cushion between the handles take the jolt out of each cut, which matters over hundreds of cuts in a day. The wire cutter near the pivot is handy for snipping old tree ties and staking wire on young trees.

Clean sap off the blades after use, a quick wipe with a solvent and a drop of oil is enough. Hone the blade with a fine stone when it stops cutting cleanly, keeping the original bevel. Check the pivot: if the blades feel loose or the cut drags, adjust the nut so the blades close smoothly without play.

Almost everything on a Felco 2 can be replaced: blade, counter blade, spring, bolt and nut. That is the real value of the tool. Instead of throwing it out when the blade chips, you replace the part and keep working.
When moving between trees on plant health care work, consider disinfecting the blades to avoid spreading disease. Shop more pruners and loppers.
A spare blade and spring in the truck means a dropped or chipped pruner is a five-minute fix, not a lost tool.

faq.q: What is the maximum branch size for the Felco 2?
faq.a: About 1 inch (25 mm) in green wood. Thicker or dead hardwood is better handled with loppers or a hand saw.

faq.q: Can I get replacement blades for the Felco 2?
faq.a: Yes. The cutting blade, counter blade, spring and most hardware are sold as spare parts.

faq.q: Is the Felco 2 good for small hands?
faq.a: It is a full-size pruner. People with smaller hands often prefer a more compact Felco model.

faq.q: How do I sharpen a Felco 2 pruner?
faq.a: Use a fine sharpening stone on the beveled side of the cutting blade, following the original angle, then remove any burr on the flat side.

name: Marvin Bull Pruner Head with Single Pulley
title: Marvin Pruner Head, Bull Model with Single Pulley
h1: Marvin Pruner Head, Bull Model with Single Pulley
meta: Marvin pruner head, Bull model, with a single pulley for heavier pole pruning cuts. How it works, fitting to your pole and keeping it sharp and safe on the job.
tagline: A heavy-duty Marvin pole pruner head with a single pulley for bigger cuts.
summary: The Bull is a heavy-duty Marvin pruner head built for thicker stems than a light pruner likes to take. A single pulley adds mechanical advantage on the rope, so you get more cutting force for each pull from the ground.
highlights: Heavy-duty Marvin pole pruner head
Single pulley adds pulling power
Bypass cut for clean pruning wounds
Mounts to a pole for ground-based work

p: A pole pruner closes when you pull the rope. On a basic head the rope acts directly on the lever. Adding a pulley gives you more force on the blade for the same pull, at the cost of a longer rope stroke. That is what you want on a heavier head like the Bull: thicker cuts without yanking so hard that the pole swings off target.
Set the hook of the head over the stem, line the blade up just outside the branch collar, and pull steadily. Let the blade do the work.
The heavier build also holds up better to the abuse pole pruners see: being hooked over limbs to pull them down, knocked against the truck and dragged through brush.

Inspect the rope for wear where it runs through the pulley and replace it before it frays through. Keep the blade sharp and the pivot clean and lightly oiled. A dull or sticky head makes you pull harder and twists the cut.
Fit the head to a pole with a matching connection, and stay away from energized lines unless you are a qualified line-clearance arborist with rated poles. See more pruners and pole pruner heads.
Keep the rope long enough to reach the ground comfortably at full pole length, and tie a stopper knot or handle at the bottom so it does not run back up.

faq.q: What does the single pulley do on a pruner head?
faq.a: It multiplies the force of your pull on the cutting lever, making thicker cuts easier but requiring a longer rope pull.

faq.q: Does the head come with a rope?
faq.a: Check the listing. If not, use a rope sized for the pulley and replace it when it shows wear.

name: Marvin Pruner Head
title: Marvin Pruner Head for Pole Pruners
meta: Marvin pruner head for building or rebuilding a pole pruner. A bypass head for clean cuts on small limbs from the ground. Fit, use and maintenance tips here.
tagline: A replacement Marvin pole pruner head for clean bypass cuts from the ground.
summary: A pruner head is the cutting end of a pole pruner, and this Marvin pruner head is a direct way to build a new pole pruner or bring a worn one back. It makes clean bypass cuts on small limbs and sprouts that are out of reach from the ground.
highlights: Bypass pole pruner head
Rope-operated cutting lever
Replaces a worn or damaged head
Clean cuts on sprouts and small limbs

body.h: Where a pole pruner fits in
p: Pole pruners handle the cuts that are too small for a pole saw and too high for hand pruners: water sprouts, suckers, small crossing limbs and fine reduction cuts. A bypass head leaves a clean wound, which is better for the tree than the crushed stub you get from a dull or anvil-style cutter.
If your current head has a bent hook, a chipped blade or a cracked casting, replacing the Marvin pruner head is usually cheaper than a new kit and gets you back to the same feel.
Marvin heads have long been part of pole pruner setups on tree crews, and a fresh head restores the snap and clean cut a worn one has lost.
Match the head to your pole fitting before ordering. Run a fresh rope, keep the blade sharp and the pivot clean, and check the bolt for play. Replace a frayed rope before it breaks mid-pull.
Keep pole tools away from energized lines unless you are a qualified line-clearance arborist with rated equipment. Pair this head with a foam-filled pole or browse more pruners and loppers.
If the blade will not close fully, check for a bent hook or debris in the pivot before you blame the rope. A small adjustment often brings a head back to clean cutting.

faq.q: What size branches can a pole pruner head cut?
faq.a: Pole pruner heads are for small limbs and sprouts. Use a pole saw for anything the blade cannot close on easily.

faq.q: Will this head fit my existing pole?
faq.a: It is made for Marvin-style fittings. Confirm the connection on your pole first.

name: Buckingham Throttle
title: Buckingham Throttle Friction Device for MRS
meta: The Buckingham Throttle is a mechanical friction device for moving rope climbing. How it compares to a friction hitch, setup cautions and inspection basics.
tagline: A mechanical friction device for climbers working moving rope systems.
summary: The Buckingham Throttle is a mechanical friction device made for moving rope system (MRS) climbing, a hardware alternative to tying and dressing a friction hitch. For climbers who want consistent friction from the first climb of the day to the last, a device like the buck throttle takes some of the variability out of the system.
highlights: Mechanical friction management for MRS climbing
More consistent feel than a hitch that wears and glazes
Made by Buckingham, a long-time arborist gear maker
Must be set up exactly per the manufacturer instructions

body.h: Why climbers move from a hitch to a device
p: A friction hitch is simple and cheap, but it changes during the day. The cord glazes, it gets wet, it tightens up after a long descent, and it needs dressing and setting. Climbers who work a lot of moving rope have been looking for hardware that gives the same feel every time, and that is the job of a mechanical device like the Buckingham Throttle.

The device manages the friction on your climbing line as you ascend, work and descend. Done right, it can make long days less tiring and descents smoother. Done wrong, any friction device can fail to hold. That is why the setup matters more than the hardware.

Buckingham has made climbing and safety gear for tree and utility workers for a long time, so the Throttle comes from a maker that knows how buckingham arborist gear gets used and abused on real jobs.

Read the manufacturer instructions before the device ever touches a rope, and follow them exactly. They specify which ropes are compatible, how the device connects to your bridge, what accessories are required, and how it must be oriented. Rope diameter, construction and coating all change how a mechanical device grips, so a rope that works in one device may not work in another.

Test the setup low and slow, on the ground or just off it, before climbing. Check that the device grabs when you weight it and releases smoothly when you want to descend. If you are new to mechanical devices, get training from an experienced climber or a qualified instructor first. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard and be used in line with ANSI Z133 and the maker's instructions.

Make sure your bridge, connectors and any tending pulley all suit the device and each other. A friction device is only one part of a system, and mismatched hardware can cross-load a carabiner or stop the device from working as designed.

Inspect before every climb. Look for wear grooves where the rope runs, cracks, bent parts, burrs and anything that moves less freely than it should. Grit in the rope wears hardware quickly, so keep your line clean. Retire the device if it shows damage or excessive wear, or if you are unsure of its history.
Pair it with a clean, compatible climbing line and see what else is in our MRS devices section.

The Throttle makes most sense for working climbers who already understand MRS well and want to fine-tune their system. Beginners are better off learning on a friction hitch first, under supervision, so they understand what the device is doing for them.
It also suits crews that want to standardize systems, so that every climber's setup works the same way and a rescue climber knows exactly what they are looking at in an aerial rescue.

faq.q: Is the Buckingham Throttle for SRS or MRS?
faq.a: It is sold for moving rope systems. Use it only in the configurations the manufacturer instructions allow.

faq.q: Which ropes can I use with the Throttle?
faq.a: Check the manufacturer instructions for the compatible rope diameters and types. Do not assume your current line is compatible.

faq.q: Does it replace training?
faq.a: No. Any life-support device requires training and a careful, supervised introduction before you trust it aloft.

name: DMM Kinisi Max Harness
title: DMM Kinisi Max Arborist Harness
meta: The DMM Kinisi Max harness is an arborist saddle built for long days of climbing and positioning. Fit, features to check and inspection basics explained here.
tagline: DMM's Kinisi arborist saddle, built for climbers who spend all day in the tree.
summary: The DMM Kinisi Max is an arborist saddle from the Kinisi line, designed for climbers who need to move freely and stay comfortable through a full day aloft. The Kinisi is built around a rope bridge, wide support and plenty of attachment points for saws and gear.
highlights: Arborist sit harness from DMM's Kinisi line
Rope bridge for free side-to-side movement
Supportive waist and leg design for long days
Gear loops and attachment points for tools

p: A saddle is the one piece of gear you are attached to all day, so comfort and freedom of movement are not luxuries. The DMM Kinisi Max saddle is built for climbers who spend hours in work position, with support where you hang and a bridge that lets you turn and reach without fighting the harness.
Attachment points for a top-handle saw, hand saw, and friction-saver or rigging gear let you set the saddle up the way you climb. Spend time adjusting it at ground level before your first climb.
The Kinisi has built a following among climbers who move a lot in the canopy, and the Max version suits those who want the platform with the features DMM put on it.

Fit is personal. Check the size range against your waist and leg measurements, and hang in it before you commit to a size. The harness should feel snug with layers on, and the bridge should sit where you can reach and tend it easily.

Inspect before each use: webbing, stitching, buckles, attachment points and especially the bridge, which is a wear item and must be replaced per DMM's instructions. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard, be used per ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer instructions, and be used only by trained climbers. Compare more saddles in European saddles.
Hang-test new adjustments low to the ground. A saddle that feels fine standing can pinch or ride up once you are in work position.

faq.q: Can I replace the bridge on the Kinisi?
faq.a: Yes. The bridge is a wear item. Replace it with the bridge DMM specifies and follow their retirement guidance.

faq.q: How do I pick the right Kinisi size?
faq.a: Use DMM's sizing chart for waist and leg measurements and, if possible, hang in the saddle before committing.

name: Petzl ASTRO BOD FAST International Harness
title: Petzl ASTRO BOD FAST International Harness
h1: Petzl ASTRO BOD FAST International Harness
meta: Petzl ASTRO BOD FAST harness, international version: a full-body harness with FAST buckles and an integrated chest ascender for rope access and rescue work.
tagline: A full-body rope access harness with an integrated chest ascender and FAST buckles.
summary: The Petzl ASTRO BOD FAST is a full-body harness built for rope access and work at height, with FAST automatic buckles and an integrated CROLL chest ascender. This is the international version of the Petzl Astro, labeled for markets outside North America.
highlights: Full-body harness for rope access and rescue
FAST automatic buckles for quick on and off
Integrated CROLL chest ascender
Multiple attachment points

p: Tree work and rope access overlap more than they used to, especially on SRT ascents, rescue setups and crane jobs. The Petzl Astro harness brings rope access features to that work: a sit harness and chest harness combined, a built-in chest ascender for efficient rope climbing, and fall-arrest attachment points.
FAST buckles let you get in and out without rethreading, which helps on long days and in cold weather.
For tree crews, the Petzl Astro is most useful as a dedicated rescue or SRT harness, or for crane and structure work where full-body fall arrest is required.
It is a heavier, more involved setup than a saddle, so plan who on the crew will use it and train them on it.

Petzl makes the ASTRO BOD FAST in versions labeled for different markets. Before you buy, confirm which version your employer, client or jurisdiction requires and check the markings on the harness itself. Use it only within the uses listed in the instructions.

Inspect webbing, stitching, buckles and the ascender before every use. Life-support gear must meet the applicable standard and be used per ANSI Z133 and Petzl's instructions, by trained users. See related fall protection gear.
Check that the CROLL teeth are clean and the cam springs back freely. Replace worn parts or the harness as Petzl directs.

faq.q: Is the Petzl ASTRO BOD FAST an arborist saddle?
faq.a: It is a rope access full-body harness. Some arborists use it for SRT and rescue, but many prefer a dedicated arborist saddle for daily climbing.

faq.q: What is the difference between the international and ANSI versions?
faq.a: They are labeled for different markets and standards. Check the markings and instructions, and choose the version your work requires.

name: Husqvarna 1 Quart Premix 50:1 Fuel, Case
title: Husqvarna 50:1 Pre-Mix 2-Stroke Fuel, 1 Quart Case
meta: Husqvarna 50:1 pre-mix 2-stroke fuel in 1 quart cans, sold by the case. Ethanol-free and ready to pour for saws and trimmers. When it beats mixing your own.
tagline: Ready-to-pour 50:1 ethanol-free premix in quart cans, sold by the case.
summary: Husqvarna 50:1 pre-mix 2-stroke fuel comes ready to pour, with ethanol-free gasoline already blended with two-stroke oil at 50:1. Buying it by the case in 1 quart cans means every saw on the truck gets the same clean fuel, and nobody is guessing at a mix ratio on the tailgate.
highlights: Pre-mixed at 50:1, no measuring
Ethanol-free gasoline
1 quart (32 fl oz) cans
Long shelf life in sealed cans
Good for saws that sit between jobs

p: Mixing your own fuel works, until someone grabs the wrong can, mixes at the wrong ratio, or fills a saw with pump gas that has been sitting in the shop for three months. Ethanol in pump gas pulls in moisture and breaks down over time. In small engines that leads to varnish, hard starts and damaged carburetors.

Husqvarna's premix removes those variables. It is ethanol-free and already blended at 50:1, so every saw, pole saw and trimmer gets the same fuel. For crews, that consistency is the main selling point. For homeowners and climbers who run a top-handle a few times a month, it means the saw starts after sitting.
It is also one less thing to carry. No oil bottles, no measuring cups, no mixing can. Grab a quart, top off the saw and go.
Two-stroke engines also run cleaner and more consistently on fresh, stable fuel, which means fewer fouled plugs and less carbon on the muffler screen over a season.

Per gallon, pre-mix costs a lot more than pump gas and oil. Most tree services do not run it in every saw every day. Where it pays off is in the saws that sit: top-handles that only come out for climbs, pole saws, backup saws on the truck, and anything that goes into storage for the season.

A common approach is to run your own mix in the big ground saws that burn a tank an hour, and pre-mix in everything else. Before storing a saw for a long stretch, many crews run it on pre-mix for a few minutes so the carburetor is full of stable fuel.

Climbers like the quart can size too. It is small enough to keep in a climbing bag or the bucket for a top-handle refill, and the sealed can does not slosh fuel the way a half-empty jug does. Some crews also keep a case on hand for winter, when saws sit longer between storm jobs and fuel goes stale fastest.

Use it in two-stroke engines that call for 50:1. Check your owner's manual. Do not use it in four-stroke engines, and do not add more oil to it. Shake the can gently before pouring if it has been sitting.

Fuel safety matters on every job: refuel with the saw shut off and cooled, away from ignition sources, and move at least 10 feet from the fueling spot before starting the saw, as recommended under ANSI Z133. Wipe up spills and keep cans closed and secured on the truck. Pair it with bar oil from our fluids section.

If a saw has been sitting on old pump-gas mix and runs poorly, draining the tank and switching to fresh pre-mix is a cheap first step before taking the carburetor apart. Many starting problems are fuel problems.

faq.q: How many cans are in a case?
faq.a: Case counts vary by listing. Check the product details for the exact number of 1 quart cans included.

faq.q: Can I use Husqvarna pre-mix in other brands of saws?
faq.a: Yes, in any two-stroke engine that calls for a 50:1 mix. Always follow your engine maker's fuel recommendations.

faq.q: How long does pre-mix last?
faq.a: Sealed cans store far longer than pump-gas mix. Once opened, keep the can tightly closed and use it within the time the label recommends.

name: Arborist Foot Loop
title: Arborist Foot Loop for Ascending and Hitch Climbing
meta: An arborist foot loop helps you stand up on the rope when ascending or advancing a hitch. Simple, light and adjustable. How climbers use it and what to check.
tagline: A simple adjustable foot loop that helps you stand and push while ascending.
summary: A foot loop is one of the simplest pieces of climbing gear and one of the most useful. Attached to a hand ascender or rope wrench setup, it lets you stand up with your legs instead of hauling with your arms, which saves a lot of energy on the climb in.
highlights: Turns arm pulls into leg pushes
Adjustable length to suit your setup
Light, packs small on the saddle
Works with hand ascenders and hitch systems

p: Your legs are much stronger than your arms. A foot loop gives them something to push against. Clip it to a hand ascender above your hitch or device, step in, stand up, and then advance your hitch or tend your system before sliding the ascender up again. It is a basic rope walking rhythm, and it is far less tiring than climbing hand over hand.
Adjust the length so that when you stand fully, your hitch or device is in easy reach. Too long and you lose the benefit, too short and you cannot get a full step.
Some climbers use two foot loops, one on each foot, while others pair one loop with a mechanical foot ascender. Both work. Start with a single loop and see how it suits your system.

A foot loop is an ascent aid, not life support. You must always be attached to your life-support system through your saddle, and your hitch or device must be tended so a slip does not drop you. Inspect the loop for cuts, abrasion and worn stitching, and retire it if in doubt.

Get trained on any ascent system before relying on it, and follow ANSI Z133 and the gear makers' instructions. For a mechanical option, see the CMI foot ascender and the rest of our foot ascenders and foot loops.
Keep the loop away from your saw and sharp edges, and store it clean and dry.

faq.q: Is a foot loop life-support equipment?
faq.a: No. It helps you ascend, but you must always be connected to a separate life-support system.

faq.q: What do I attach a foot loop to?
faq.a: Usually a hand ascender on the rope, positioned above your hitch or friction device.

name: CMI Foot Ascender
title: CMI Foot Ascender for SRT Rope Climbing
meta: The CMI foot ascender lets you rope walk on SRT with a natural stepping motion. Left and right versions, setup basics, inspection and who it is meant for.
tagline: A boot-mounted rope ascender that turns every step into upward progress.
summary: The CMI foot ascender mounts to your boot and grabs the rope each time you step, so climbing a single rope feels closer to walking up stairs than pulling yourself up. For climbers who ascend SRT into big trees, a foot ascender is often the biggest energy saver in the system.
highlights: Boot-mounted ascender for SRT ascents
Turns leg drive into steady upward progress
Keeps the tail of the rope weighted below your system
Made by CMI, a long-standing US rope gear maker
Pairs with a hand ascender or chest ascender system
specs: Ascent aid, not primary life support

p: Single rope ascent is mostly about how efficiently you turn leg strength into height. With a foot ascender on one boot, every step grabs the rope and holds your gain, while your hitch or device slides up behind it. It also keeps the rope tensioned below you, so your upper system feeds smoothly without a hand dedicated to pulling slack.

Climbers who ascend 60 or 80 feet into a big tree several times a day notice the difference fast. Less arm work on the way up means more energy for the actual job: rigging, cutting and moving through the canopy.

It also helps when you change direction in the tree. Because the foot ascender keeps tension on the rope below you, your device or hitch moves more cleanly, and you spend less time fiddling with slack and more time getting to work position. Over a full day of foot ascenders and multiple climbs, the savings in arm strength are obvious.

Most climbers wear the foot ascender on one foot and a foot loop or knee ascender on the other side, combined with a chest-mounted device or hitch on the saddle. The exact setup depends on your system, and you should match it to what you have been trained on. Strap it securely to a stiff-soled boot so it does not roll off when you step.

Check the rope diameter range and compatibility in CMI's instructions before using it on your line. Practice low to the ground until the stepping rhythm feels natural and the release is second nature, especially for the moment you transition from ascent to work position.

Before you leave the ground, check how the rope runs from your upper device past the foot ascender. Twists in the line or a strap that rides up your boot will make each step awkward. A few practice steps low down sort that out quickly.
When you reach your tie-in, many climbers flip the foot ascender off the rope so it does not catch on branches while they work. Get comfortable doing that with gloves on.

A foot ascender is an ascent aid, not your life support. You must always be connected to your saddle through your primary system, and that system must meet the applicable standard and be used per ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer's instructions. Get training before you add any mechanical ascender to your climbing.

Inspect before each use for wear on the cam teeth, cracks, a weak spring, and frayed or cut straps. Clean out grit and sap, which can stop the cam from biting. Retire it if you see damage. Pair it with an arborist foot loop or a knee ascender for a full rope walking setup.

faq.q: Do I need a left or right foot ascender?
faq.a: Most climbers wear it on their dominant foot, but it is personal preference. Order the version that matches the foot you plan to use.

faq.q: Can I use a foot ascender on any climbing rope?
faq.a: Check CMI's instructions for compatible rope diameters and types before use.

faq.q: Is a foot ascender required for SRT?
faq.a: No, but it makes ascents much more efficient, especially on long climbs.

name: SAKA Foldable Knee Ascender
title: SAKA Foldable Knee Ascender for Rope Walking
meta: The SAKA foldable knee ascender adds a second gripping point for rope walking ascents and folds away when you reach your work position. Setup and safety tips.
tagline: A knee ascender for efficient rope walking that folds away once you are up.
summary: A knee ascender rides on the rope below your chest system and is linked to your knee or shin, so each step on that side drives you up. The SAKA knee ascender folds when you are done ascending, which keeps it out of the way while you work.
highlights: Adds a second step to your rope walking system
Foldable to stay out of the way at work
Pairs well with a foot ascender
Ascent aid for SRT climbers

body.h: How a knee ascender fits a rope walker
p: Rope walking systems pair a foot ascender on one leg with a knee ascender on the other. As you step with each leg in turn, one of them always holds the gain. It is smooth, steady and easy on your arms, which is why it is popular for long climbs into tall trees.
The SAKA's folding design matters once you reach your tie-in point. Instead of a device flapping around your shin while you work, you fold it and get on with the job.

Because a knee ascender is linked to your leg rather than strapped under your boot, it moves with your shin as you step. That gives a long, efficient stroke on each step and a steady rhythm on long ascents.

A knee ascender is an ascent aid. You must always be attached through your primary life-support system, which must meet the applicable standard and be used per ANSI Z133 and the manufacturer instructions. Learn rope walking with a trained climber, low to the ground, before using it on a real ascent.
Inspect the cam, frame and straps before every use. Pair it with the CMI foot ascender for a complete rope walking setup.
Clean grit and sap out of the cam after dirty days so it keeps biting cleanly on the rope.

faq.q: Do I need a foot ascender with a knee ascender?
faq.a: They are designed to work together in a rope walking setup, one on each leg.

faq.q: Is the SAKA knee ascender life support?
faq.a: No. It is an ascent aid. Stay attached to your primary life-support system at all times.

name: 9/16" Dead Eye Rigging Sling
title: 9/16" Dead Eye Sling for Tree Rigging
meta: A 9/16-inch dead eye sling for tree rigging: choke it around a spar or limb and hang a block or rigging line. How to use it, inspect it and when to retire it.
tagline: A 9/16-inch rope sling with a spliced eye for setting rigging points.
summary: A dead eye sling is a length of rigging rope with a spliced eye on one end and a plain tail on the other. Pass the tail through the eye to choke it around a spar, then hang a block or tie off your rigging line. At 9/16 inch, it suits medium rigging work.
highlights: 9/16-inch rope sling with spliced eye
Chokes around a stem or limb
Hang blocks, rings or lowering devices
Simple, quick rigging point

body.h: How a dead eye sling is used
p: The dead eye sling is the quickest way to make an anchor in a tree. Wrap it around the stem, pass the tail through the eye to form a choke, and tie a secure hitch to attach a block or tie the rigging line. It works for setting a lowering point, a redirect or a natural crotch backup.
Choose the sling length to suit the stem diameter you usually work, and keep a few lengths on the truck.

Dead eye slings are also handy for setting a temporary anchor on a spar during a removal, or as a sling for a lowering device on the trunk. Rotate slings through use so one is not taking all the hard loads.

Rigging loads are dynamic, and the forces on an anchor can be much higher than the weight of the piece. Size the sling to the loads you will generate, use the manufacturer's rated strength, and stay within a sensible working load. Never use a rigging sling as life support.
Inspect before each use for cuts, glazing, crushed sections and a worn splice. Retire slings that have been shock-loaded hard or show damage. More options in heavy-duty slings.
Store slings clean, dry and out of the sun. UV, grit and chemicals all weaken rope over time.

faq.q: What is the difference between a dead eye sling and an eye-and-eye sling?
faq.a: A dead eye has one spliced eye and a plain tail. An eye-and-eye has spliced eyes at both ends and is used for girth hitches and basket rigging.

faq.q: Can I climb on a rigging sling?
faq.a: No. Rigging slings are not life-support equipment.

name: Helmet Ear Muff
title: Helmet Ear Muffs for Arborist and Chainsaw Helmets
meta: Helmet ear muffs clip into slotted arborist and chainsaw helmets to protect your hearing on noisy jobs. Fit, noise ratings and wearing tips explained here.
tagline: Clip-on ear muffs for slotted helmets, for saw, chipper and grinder work.
summary: Helmet ear muffs clip directly into the side slots of a work helmet, so hearing protection is always on your head and ready to flip down. For tree crews running saws, chippers and stump grinders all day, that convenience is what keeps people wearing them.
highlights: Clips into slotted work helmets
Flip up when talking, down when cutting
Always with the helmet, so it does not get left on the truck
Works with face screens on most helmets
Replaceable cushions on most models

body.h: Why hearing protection on the helmet makes sense
p: Chainsaws, chippers and stump grinders are loud enough to damage hearing in a single workday without protection. Hearing loss from noise is permanent and creeps up slowly, so by the time you notice, it is too late. The best protection is the one you actually wear every time.

That is the argument for earmuffs under helmet setups, or more precisely, mounted on the helmet. They are always there. You do not have to find them in the truck or pull them out of a pocket. Flip them down when the saw starts, flip them up to talk to the ground crew.

Hearing protection also helps with fatigue. A day of saw noise wears you down, and people who protect their hearing often report feeling less drained at the end of a long job. That matters on a crew where focus is safety.
Muffs also make it easier to hear the important things. With the saw noise knocked down, many workers find shouted commands and whistle signals from the ground clearer, not harder, to pick out.

On a typical removal, the climber's top-handle, the ground saw, the chipper and maybe a loader or grinder are all running within a few minutes of each other. Even crew members who are not running a saw are exposed, so everyone on site should have protection on.

Helmet ear muffs clip into the accessory slots on the side of a helmet. Most climbing and forestry helmets use a standard slot, but not all do, so check your helmet before ordering. Once fitted, adjust the arms so the cups seal fully around your ears with no gaps. Hair, glasses arms and hats under the helmet all reduce the seal.
If you wear a face screen, make sure the muffs and screen work together and the muffs can still reach the work position. See our helmets for slotted models that accept muffs and visors.
Helmet ear muffs also stay put when you look up, bend over or climb, which is where loose headband muffs tend to slip. For climbers, that means one less thing moving around while you work.

body.h: Choosing and caring for ear muffs
p: Every hearing protector carries a noise reduction rating (NRR) on the label. Higher is more protection, but real-world protection is lower than the label figure, especially with a poor seal. For very loud work like grinding, some crews double up with foam ear plugs under the muffs.

Replace the ear cushions and foam inserts when they harden, crack or flatten, since that ruins the seal. Keep the muffs clean and dry. Check that the arms still hold tension. If the cups feel loose on your head, they are not protecting you.
Keep a spare set of cushions in the truck, so a cracked seal does not mean a day of working without protection.

faq.q: Will these ear muffs fit my helmet?
faq.a: They fit helmets with standard side accessory slots. Confirm your helmet's slot style before ordering.

faq.q: Can I wear ear plugs with helmet ear muffs?
faq.a: Yes. For very loud work, plugs plus muffs give more protection than either alone.

faq.q: How often should I replace the ear cushions?
faq.a: Whenever they crack, harden or no longer seal, and at least as often as the maker recommends.

name: Bigfoot Composite Outrigger Pads
title: Bigfoot Outrigger Pads, Composite, for Bucket Trucks
meta: Bigfoot outrigger pads spread the load of bucket truck and crane outriggers over soft ground and protect lawns and drives. Sizing, use and inspection tips here.
tagline: Composite outrigger pads that spread the load under bucket trucks and cranes.
summary: Bigfoot outrigger pads go under the feet of a bucket truck, crane or knuckle-boom outrigger to spread the load over a larger area. That keeps the machine level and stable on soft ground and protects lawns, driveways and pavers from punched-in dents.
highlights: Spreads outrigger load over a larger footprint
Composite construction, no rot or splinters
Protects lawns, drives and hardscape
Built-in handles for carrying (model dependent)

p: A bucket truck or crane puts a huge point load on each outrigger foot. On soft lawn, wet ground or thin asphalt, a foot can sink or punch through, and a machine that settles mid-lift is a serious hazard. Pads spread that load, so the ground pressure drops and the machine stays where you set it.
Composite Bigfoot crane pads also do not rot, soak up water or split like wood cribbing, and they clean off with a hose.
Composite pads are also lighter to handle than steel plates, so one person can usually set and pick up pads without a struggle.

Size pads to the machine and the ground. Larger pads are needed for heavier machines and softer soils. Check the equipment manufacturer's requirements and do not exceed the pad's rating. Center the outrigger foot on the pad, set it on firm, level ground where you can, and recheck after the first lift.
Inspect pads for cracks and deep gouges and replace damaged ones. See more bucket truck accessories and ground protection mats.
Keep the pads with the truck at all times, not in the shop. The day you leave them behind is the day the ground turns out softer than it looked.

faq.q: What size outrigger pad do I need?
faq.a: It depends on the machine's outrigger load and the ground conditions. Follow the equipment maker's guidance and the pad's rated capacity.

faq.q: Are composite pads better than wood?
faq.a: They do not rot or absorb water, they are easy to clean and they last longer, though they cost more up front.

name: Weaver Two-Man Bucket Truck Cover
title: Weaver Two-Man Bucket Truck Cover
meta: Weaver bucket truck cover for two-man buckets keeps rain, snow and debris out of the bucket between jobs and on the road. Fit, features and care explained.
tagline: A cover for two-man aerial buckets that keeps weather and debris out.
summary: A bucket truck cover keeps rain, snow, leaves and road grime out of the bucket when the truck is parked or traveling. This Weaver cover is sized for two-man buckets, so it suits the larger aerial lifts many tree and utility crews run.
highlights: Sized for two-man buckets
Keeps water and debris out of the bucket
Protects the bucket liner and controls
Quick on and off at the start and end of the day

p: An uncovered bucket collects water, ice, leaves and sawdust. That is bad for the bucket liner, the controls and the gear you leave inside. Water standing in a bucket also adds weight and can freeze overnight in winter. A bucket truck bucket cover is a simple fix, and on the road it keeps loose items from blowing out.
Weaver has been making gear for linemen and tree crews for a long time, and this cover is built to be thrown on and pulled off daily.
It also keeps the bucket cleaner for the next morning, so the crew is not scooping out wet leaves before they can go up.

Two-man buckets vary in size, so measure yours and compare it with the listing before ordering. Secure the cover so it does not flap at highway speed. Let it dry before rolling it up, and keep it away from saws and sharp gear.
Never leave the cover on during operation. Browse more bucket truck accessories.
Shake out debris before you put it on, and check the tie-downs and fasteners regularly. A cover that blows off on the highway is a hazard to other drivers.
Remove the cover fully before any lift, so it cannot snag a control or blow into the boom.

faq.q: Will this cover fit a one-man bucket?
faq.a: It is sized for two-man buckets. A one-man bucket needs a smaller cover.

faq.q: Can I drive with the cover on?
faq.a: Yes, as long as it is properly secured. Remove it before operating the bucket.

name: Wheel Chock
keyword: chock the wheels of a truck
title: Wheel Chock: How to Chock the Wheels of a Truck
h1: Wheel Chock: Chock the Wheels of a Truck
meta: A heavy-duty wheel chock for bucket trucks, chip trucks and trailers. Why and how to chock the wheels of a truck on every job, and how many chocks to use.
tagline: A heavy-duty wheel chock for tree trucks, chippers and trailers.
summary: Every crew should chock the wheels of a truck before anyone gets out of the cab to work. A wheel chock is cheap, simple and one of the most important safety items on a tree service truck, especially on bucket trucks, chip trucks and any vehicle parked on a grade.
highlights: Holds parked trucks and trailers in place
Sized for work trucks and equipment
Handle or rope for easy placement and retrieval
High-visibility color on most models
Sold individually, buy at least two per vehicle

body.h: Why chocks matter on a tree job
p: Parking brakes fail, transmissions get bumped out of park, and ground shifts under a loaded truck. A bucket truck that rolls while someone is in the bucket, or a chip truck that rolls into the chipper crew, is a catastrophic accident that a pair of chocks prevents. That is why most companies and many standards require chocks on any vehicle that is parked for work.
Wheel chocks also tell everyone on site that the truck is set up and not moving. Make placing them part of your arrival routine, along with cones, signs and setting up the work zone.

Tree trucks are often parked on residential streets with a crown, on driveways with a slope, or on soft shoulders. Each of those increases the chance of a vehicle creeping, especially once the chipper is running and the truck is vibrating.
Chocks matter for chippers too. A towed chipper parked on a slope with the truck unhooked has nothing holding it but its own jack, and a rolling chipper is as dangerous as a rolling truck.

body.h: How to chock the wheels correctly
p: Set the parking brake first. Then place the chocks snug against the tires on the downhill side, so gravity pushes the tire into the chock. On level ground, chock both front and back of one tire. On a slope, chock the downhill side of both rear tires, or follow your company and vehicle maker's procedures if they call for more.

For bucket trucks, chock before you set the outriggers and do not pull the chocks until the boom is stowed and the outriggers are up. On a trailer or chipper, chock the trailer wheels before unhitching. Always remove the chocks before you drive off. A lot of crews hang a tag on the steering wheel as a reminder.
Train everyone on the crew to do it, not just the driver. When chocking is a habit the whole crew owns, it does not get skipped on the rushed jobs, which are exactly the ones that go wrong.

Pick a chock sized for your tire diameter and vehicle weight. Small chocks made for cars or campers will roll right over on a heavy truck. Rubber and polyurethane chocks grip well on pavement and do not split. A handle or rope makes them easy to pull out from under a truck. Bright colors help you find them and help others see them.
Keep them in a fixed spot on the truck so they are always easy to grab. See more bucket truck accessories, including outrigger pads for soft ground.
Inspect chocks now and then for cracks, chunks missing from the face and worn handles, and replace them when they no longer sit flat against the tire.
Some crews pair a chock with a small cone so the chocked wheel is easy to spot from the cab before driving away.

faq.q: How many wheel chocks should a truck have?
faq.a: At least two. Many crews carry more for trailers, chippers and work on steep grades.

faq.q: Which side of the tire do chocks go on?
faq.a: On the downhill side, so the tire would roll into the chock. On level ground, chock both sides of one tire.

faq.q: Do I still need chocks if the parking brake is set?
faq.a: Yes. Chocks are a backup for brake or transmission failure, and many company policies require both.

name: Bucket Truck Chainsaw Scabbard
title: Chainsaw Scabbard for Bucket Truck and Aerial Lifts
h1: Chainsaw Scabbard for Bucket Truck and Aerial Lifts
meta: A chainsaw scabbard for bucket truck and aerial lift work holds your saw on the bucket lip, ready to grab and out of your way. Fit, mounting and safety tips.
tagline: A bucket-mounted saw holder that keeps a chainsaw secure and in reach aloft.
summary: A chainsaw scabbard for bucket truck work hangs on the bucket lip and holds your saw bar-down, so it is ready when you need it and out of the way when you do not. It keeps the saw off the bucket floor, away from your legs, and out of the controls.
highlights: Hangs on the side of the bucket
Holds the saw bar-down and secure
Keeps the saw off the floor and away from controls
Fits top-handle and small rear-handle saws (check bar length)
Drain openings so sawdust and water fall through

body.h: Why a scabbard belongs on every bucket
p: A bucket is a small space. Two people, a saw, a pole saw, a hand saw and maybe a rope all share it. A running or recently stopped chainsaw lying on the floor is a cut risk to your legs and can bump into the controls. A bucket truck chainsaw scabbard solves that. The saw hangs outside the working space, bar down, and you can grab it with one hand.

It also protects the saw. Saws knocking around on the bucket floor get chains dulled and covers cracked. In the scabbard, the chain is shielded and the saw is not rattling around while you move the boom.
On the ground, the same scabbard keeps the saw secure on the truck between bucket setups, and it means the saw always lives in the same place, which helps every crew member find it without looking.
It also gives your hands back. With the saw hung outside the bucket, you have both hands for positioning the boom, handling a pole saw or tying off a piece for a controlled lower.

Check that the scabbard fits the lip of your bucket and the saw you run. Most work with top-handle saws and compact rear-handle saws, but bar length and powerhead size vary, so compare the listing with your saw. Mount it on the side away from the controls and where it will not catch on limbs as you boom through the canopy.
Some crews run two: one for the top-handle and one for a pole saw or hand saw. Keep the chainsaw holder for the bucket truck clear of hydraulic lines and the platform gate.
If you run a two-man bucket, agree on which side the saw lives on so both operators know where it is and nobody reaches across the controls for it.
A bucket truck chainsaw scabbard with drain openings stays lighter and cleaner, since rain and sawdust fall through rather than collecting around the bar.

Always engage the chain brake before putting the saw in the scabbard, and never put a running saw away. In the bucket, follow ANSI Z133 and your employer's procedures, wear your fall protection attached to the designated anchor, and keep a safe distance from energized lines unless you are a qualified line-clearance arborist.
Clean the scabbard out regularly so sawdust and sap do not pack in. See related gear in bucket truck accessories and chainsaw cases.

Check the scabbard for cracks, worn hooks and loose hardware during your daily truck inspection. A scabbard that pops off the bucket lip drops a saw on whoever is below, so replace it as soon as it no longer seats firmly. Keep the work zone below the bucket clear of ground workers whenever you are cutting or handling the saw aloft.

faq.q: Will a bucket truck scabbard fit my saw?
faq.a: Most fit top-handle and compact saws. Check the bar length and powerhead size against the listing.

faq.q: How do I mount a chainsaw scabbard on a bucket?
faq.a: It hooks over the bucket lip. Place it away from the controls and where it will not snag on branches.

faq.q: Can I put the saw away with the engine running?
faq.a: No. Shut the saw off, engage the chain brake, then put it in the scabbard.

name: 6' Web Retractable Fall Protection Lanyard
title: Retractable Safety Harness Lanyard, 6' Web
meta: A 6-foot web retractable lanyard to pair with your retractable safety harness setup. Where it works, where it does not, and the checks to run before each use.
tagline: A 6-foot self-retracting web lanyard for fall protection at height.
summary: A retractable lanyard is the piece that turns a fall arrest harness into a retractable safety harness system: the web pays out as you move and locks if you fall. This 6-foot web unit keeps slack off the floor while letting you move around your work area.
highlights: 6-foot self-retracting web lifeline
Takes up slack automatically as you move
Locks quickly in a fall
Compact and light compared with cable units

p: A retractable lanyard harness setup is common on rooftops, platforms and structures where you move around an anchor above you. Because it keeps the line short, it limits free fall distance compared with a standard shock-absorbing lanyard.

In aerial lifts, check carefully before using any self-retracting device. Bucket anchorages are often at or below the waist, and many retractables are rated only for overhead anchorage. Use only equipment the lift manufacturer and the device's instructions allow for that use.
A web lifeline is lighter and less bulky than a cable unit, and it is easier on surfaces it rubs against.

Before each use, pull the web out fully and check it for cuts, burns and fraying, test that it locks with a sharp tug, and check the housing and connectors. Remove from service any unit that has arrested a fall or fails a check.

Fall protection must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133 where it applies, and be used by trained workers. See other fall arrest gear for aerial lifts.
Keep the housing clean, store it out of the weather and never let the web retract uncontrolled.
Read the label for the device's capacity and the anchorage it is rated for before first use.

faq.q: Can I use a retractable lanyard in a bucket truck?
faq.a: Only if the device is rated for the anchorage position in your bucket and the lift maker allows it. Many are rated for overhead anchorage only.

faq.q: What harness do I use with it?
faq.a: A full-body fall arrest harness, connected at the attachment point specified in the instructions.

name: Petzl ABSORBICA-I Energy Absorbing Lanyard
title: Petzl ABSORBICA-I Energy Absorbing Lanyard
meta: Petzl ABSORBICA-I is a single energy-absorbing lanyard for fall arrest. Lengths, connectors, how it limits fall forces and when to remove it from service.
tagline: A single-leg energy-absorbing lanyard for fall arrest at height.
summary: The Petzl ABSORBICA-I is a single-leg lanyard with a built-in energy absorber. In a fall, the absorber tears open to cut the force on your body and your anchor. The Petzl Absorbica line is compact and light, which makes it easy to carry on a full-body harness.
highlights: Single-leg fall arrest lanyard
Built-in energy absorber limits fall forces
Available in different lengths and connector options
Compact absorber pack

p: An energy absorber is a pack of webbing stitched so it rips apart in a controlled way during a fall. That spreads the stopping force out over a short distance, reducing the peak load on your body. After it deploys, the lanyard is done and must be retired.
Absorber lanyards need clearance below you to work, since the absorber extends during a fall. Check the clearance requirements in Petzl's instructions before you anchor.
Choose the length to suit your setup. A shorter lanyard limits how far you can move from the anchor but also reduces fall distance.
Plan your anchor position so the lanyard is never slack across an edge, and never tie a knot in it to shorten it.

In aerial lifts, use the anchorage, harness and lanyard combination allowed by the lift manufacturer and your employer, and check the lanyard's length against the platform. Inspect before each use: webbing, stitching, the absorber pack, and connectors. Any sign of deployment means retirement.
Fall protection must meet the applicable standard and be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133 by trained workers. See more fall arrest gear for aerial lifts.
Store the lanyard dry and away from chemicals and sharp gear, and record when it entered service.
Check that the connectors gate fully and lock every time.

faq.q: Can I reuse an ABSORBICA after a fall?
faq.a: No. Once the absorber has deployed, even partly, the lanyard must be removed from service.

faq.q: Is the ABSORBICA-I a positioning lanyard?
faq.a: No. It is a fall arrest lanyard. Use a dedicated adjustable lanyard for work positioning.

name: Safewaze Economy Fall Protection Kit
title: Safewaze Fall Protection Economy Kit
meta: Safewaze fall protection economy kit: a basic harness and lanyard package for aerial lifts and general work at height. What to check, fit and training notes.
tagline: A budget-friendly harness and lanyard kit for aerial lift crews.
summary: This Safewaze fall protection kit packages the basics for working from an aerial lift or other elevated platform at an economy price. It is a sensible way to outfit a new crew member or keep spare sets on the truck.
highlights: Harness and lanyard package
Economy price for outfitting crews
Good for spare sets on the truck
From Safewaze, a fall protection maker
specs: Aerial lifts, general work at height

body.h: What a kit is good for
p: Buying a matched harness and lanyard together means the pieces are designed to work together and you are not guessing at compatibility. For companies adding bucket trucks or lifts, or putting new hires in the bucket, an economy kit gets everyone properly equipped without a long shopping list.
Check the kit contents and the lanyard type in the listing, and make sure they suit how your crew uses lifts.
Because the price is lower, there is less temptation to keep using a harness that should have been retired. Replace worn gear rather than stretching it.
Keep a written log of each kit's inspections.

A harness only works when it fits. Adjust leg straps and chest strap snug, with the back D-ring between the shoulder blades. Inspect webbing, stitching, buckles, D-rings and the lanyard before every use, and retire anything that has arrested a fall or shows damage.

Fall protection must meet the applicable standard, be used per the manufacturer's instructions and ANSI Z133 where it applies, and be used by trained workers. Compare options in fall arrest for aerial lifts.
Label each kit and assign it to one worker when you can, so fit adjustments stay set and inspections are easy to track.

faq.q: Is this kit suitable for tree climbing?
faq.a: No. It is fall arrest gear for platforms and lifts. Tree climbing requires an arborist saddle and climbing system.

faq.q: How often should I replace a harness?
faq.a: Follow the manufacturer's service life guidance and retire it right away after a fall or any damage.

name: Ground Protection Mats, 3' x 8'
title: HDPE Ground Protection Mats, 3' x 8'
meta: HDPE ground protection mats in a 3x8 size that one or two people can handle. Protect lawns and soft ground under trucks and loaders. Specs and use tips.
tagline: A 3 x 8 foot HDPE mat for protecting turf and soft ground on tree jobs.
summary: HDPE ground protection mats lay down a temporary road for trucks, loaders and stump grinders, spreading the load so you do not leave ruts in a client's lawn. The 3 x 8 foot size is easy for a crew to carry and place.
highlights: 3 x 8 ft high-density polyethylene mat
Spreads load from trucks and compact equipment
Traction tread for tires and tracks
Easy for a crew to carry and place

p: Repairing ruts in a lawn or replacing broken pavers costs money and costs you the client. HDPE ground mats stop that before it starts. They spread the weight of a mini skid steer, a stump grinder or a chip truck tire over a larger area, so the ground underneath stays intact.
The 3 x 8 ground protection mats size is a handy one. It is light enough for one or two people to move, narrow enough for gates and side yards, and you can lay several in a line to build a path.
Lay them across a lawn to get a chipper or mini loader to the back of the property, or under the tires of a truck parked on soft ground.
Lay mats on ground that is as level as possible, overlap or connect them so edges do not lift, and run tires down the center. Check the load rating against your heaviest machine.
Hose them off before loading so you do not track mud onto the next job, and stack them flat. See the full range of ground protection mats.
Inspect for cracks and torn connector holes before laying them, and replace damaged mats so edges do not catch tires or boots.

faq.q: Can a bucket truck drive on 3x8 mats?
faq.a: Check the mat's load rating against your truck's axle weight. Many crews use larger or thicker mats for heavy trucks.

faq.q: Do HDPE mats work on wet ground?
faq.a: Yes. That is when they help most, since soft ground ruts easily.

name: Ground Protection Mats
title: Ground Mats for Tree Crews: Protect Lawns and Turf
h1: Ground Mats: HDPE Ground Protection Mats
meta: Ground mats protect lawns, turf and soft ground under trucks, loaders and stump grinders. HDPE mat sizes, load ratings and how tree crews use them on site.
tagline: HDPE ground mats that keep trucks and equipment from rutting a client's yard.
summary: Ground mats are the difference between leaving a clean yard and leaving a muddy mess with ruts that need regrading. These HDPE ground protection mats give your trucks, loaders and stump grinders a temporary roadway over turf and soft ground, and they lift and move as the job progresses.
highlights: High-density polyethylene, no rot or splinters
Spreads load from trucks and heavy equipment
Traction tread for tires and tracks
Reusable job after job
Works as lawn protection mats on finished turf
specs: Turf, soft ground and hardscape protection

p: Most residential tree removals happen in a back yard. Getting a loader, chip truck or stump grinder back there means crossing lawn, irrigation and sometimes pavers. Without protection, one wet day can leave ruts that take a landscaper a week to fix. A ground protection mat spreads the load so the ground under it barely notices.
Mats also save time. Instead of hand-carrying brush across a soft lawn, you can bring the machine to the work. That alone pays for a set of mats over a season.
Clients notice, too. Showing up with mats tells a homeowner you plan to leave the yard the way you found it, and that is often what wins the next job.
